doc.title: JJ Johnson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Jam sessions at Minton's
summary: The famed trumpet night with Dizzy, Webster, Navarro, Miles and McGhee; unrecorded jams; no trombone night.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Tell us about the jam sessions at Minton’s.

They were mind-boggling to say the least – most of them – because you would have the top practitioners of the genre, shall we say, stopping in just to have some fun. I think the one that stands out in my mind over all the others was, on this particular

occasion, the night for trumpet players to have a go at it. On this given night there was Dizzy, Freddie Webster, Fats Navarro, Miles Davis, and a fifth trumpet player – it may have been Howard McGee. Words could not ever describe what happened on the bandstand with these five trumpet players having a go at it. It was something not to be believed. I still don’t believe it. It's too bad it wasn’t recorded, and it wasn’t. The jam sessions that took place at Minton’s, I don’t [know that] they were ever [recorded]. Are there any recordings, like jam [sessions], [that] you know of?
Yeah. Wire recordings.
Wire recordings. Oh, not actual recordings under ideal conditions that we would know about of jam sessions that took place, [recordings] at those wonderful, wonderful jam sessions.
They released quite a few of them.
There would be a tenor saxophone night. There'd be a trumpet night. There would be a night where piano players were . . .
Charlie Christian on some of them – 1944 with Monk and Dizzy.
On a wire recording?
Yes. Released later, but done with a wire recorder.
It was some guy in the audience.
Yeah.
Unauthorized.
Because it was such a new phenomena, guys would just set the big old recorder up, just like Gene Fowlkes.
They were hiding it, yeah, yeah.

So that would have been around this time. Was it common for other trombonists? I can’t imagine any other trombone players showing up at those sessions because that was pretty fast company, I mean, to try to play those tunes.
I don’t remember there ever being a trombone night. I’m not saying it didn’t
happen. I have no recollection of it. I don’t recall there ever being a night where the trombone players of the day were having a go at it. I don’t remember there ever being such a night.
I don’t think there were many equipped to handle the music, [especially if someone would] call a tune like Bebop.
Oh, my goodness, yeah.
Everybody had to go to the bathroom. Right quick!
[laughs] Yeah.
